title: Scenario-based and Mental Maths
lines: About 6 of USAT's 25 quantitative questions are everyday scenarios or quick mental sums: shopping in a bazaar, bus and train timetables, mobile packages, cricket run rates, cooking for guests, calendars and clocks, unit rates, and people or machines working together. None needs advanced mathematics. They test whether you can pick out the numbers that matter and calculate cleanly without a calculator.
## A routine for every scenario
- Underline what is asked (the change, the time, the rate) before reading the numbers.
- Put everything in one unit: grams or kilograms, minutes or hours, MB or GB.
- Estimate the answer, then calculate, then compare with the options.
## Shopping and unit rates
- Compare value by the price of one unit: Rs per kg, Rs per litre, Rs per GB.
- 'Buy 2, get 1 free' means you pay for 2 out of every 3.
- Rate × quantity = cost; distance ÷ fuel per km gives litres.
## Time, timetables and calendars
- Add hours first, then minutes, and carry 60 minutes as 1 hour. Crossing midnight: work out time to midnight, then add the rest.
- A day of the week repeats every 7 days. 45 days later is 45 mod 7 = 3 days on.
- An ordinary year moves dates on by 1 weekday; a leap year by 2.
- Month lengths: 30 days in April, June, September and November; February 28 (29 in a leap year); the rest 31.
- Clock angle at h:m = |30h − 5.5m| degrees, taking the smaller angle if it exceeds 180°.
## Cricket rates
- Run rate = runs ÷ overs. An over has 6 balls, so 12.2 overs means 12 overs and 2 balls, which is 74 balls or 12⅓ overs.
- Required rate = runs still needed ÷ overs left.
- Strike rate = runs ÷ balls × 100. Batting average = runs ÷ number of times out.
## Work and rates
- If A takes a hours and B takes b hours, together they do 1/a + 1/b of the job per hour.
- If rates are given as amounts per hour (boxes, bottles), simply add them.
## Mental-maths toolkit
| Trick | Example
| Near a round number | 99 × 46 = 4,600 − 46 = 4,554
| Difference of squares | 39 × 41 = 40² − 1 = 1,599
| Square ending in 5 | 85²: 8 × 9 = 72, write 25: 7,225
| Halve and double | 16 × 35 = 8 × 70 = 560
| Percent by pieces | 15 % of 480 = 48 + 24 = 72
- Fractions of amounts: find one part first. 3/8 of 320 is 3 × 40 = 120.
- Estimation: round each number to one significant figure and multiply. 302 × 49 is about 300 × 50 = 15,000.
## Worked examples
> A train leaves Rawalpindi at 21:45 and the journey takes 14 h 30 min. When does it arrive?
> 21:45 to midnight is 2 h 15 min. 14 h 30 min − 2 h 15 min = 12 h 15 min, so it arrives at 12:15 the next day.
> Chasing 160 in 20 overs, a team is 70 for 2 after 10 overs. What rate is now needed?
> Runs needed = 90 in 10 overs, so 9 runs per over.
> A recipe for 8 people uses 600 g of meat. How much is needed for 14 people?
> 600 ÷ 8 = 75 g per person, and 14 × 75 = 1,050 g, that is 1.05 kg.
> A 500 ml juice pack costs Rs 90 and a 1.5 litre bottle costs Rs 240. Which is cheaper per litre, and by how much?
> Small: Rs 180 per litre. Large: 240 ÷ 1.5 = Rs 160 per litre. The bottle is Rs 20 per litre cheaper.
! Decimal hours are not minutes: 2.5 hours is 2 h 30 min, not 2 h 50 min.
! 12.2 overs is not 12.2 in arithmetic. Change to balls (74) or to 12⅓ overs.
! In 'every 30 seconds or part of it' charges, round the number of units up.
! Read whether the question wants the total or the rate, the saving per item or the whole saving.
## Quick check
- Can you work out 101 × 47 in your head? (4,747)
- What day is it 50 days after a Friday? (Saturday)
- What is the run rate for 150 runs in 18 overs? (8⅓)
- How many minutes is 0.75 of an hour? (45)
